newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia keeps silent on telecom privatisation plans.
newsitem.headline: Serbia keeps silent on telecom privatisation plans.

text.p: Privatisation of Serbia's post and telecommunications company announced for March seems to be heading for an early start, but apart from the timing it has nothing in common with the company's original plans.

Economists told Reuters on Wednesday they were worried that what was once billed as a big public sale involving an employee shareholding and foreign tenders might be rushed through in secret to win the cash-strapped state hard currency to pay overdue pensions and salaries.

PTT Srbija declined to confirm a statement on Tuesday from Italian state telecommunications holding Stet that the two sides were discussing the sale of a 49 percent stake in PTT Srbija to the Italian firm.

"That is what they want. But we do not negotiate. It is the government who negotiates and we would certainly not want to comment on anybody's wishes and plans," said a high-ranking PTT Srbija offical, speaking under condition of anonymity.
The Financial Times, citing Serbian officials, said on Tuesday Stet was expected to buy 49 percent of PTT Srbija for between $610 million and $900 million.
Preliminary estimates prepared by the Belgrade-based private institute for economic research CES-Mecon valued the Serbian telecommunications unit at around $5 billion.
The value of the stake prepared for sale to the Italian company ranged between $1.4 billion and $2.8 billion.
"It is certain that the government has decided to sell a 49 percent stake in the PTT, matching the limit set by the federal privatisation law," an economist said.
The 49 percent stake was far more than the PTT's recently sacked general manager Milorad Jaksic was prepared to offer.

Announcing the company's privatisation plans last November, Jaksic said selling up to 30 percent in the first round would be best. He also wanted privatisation that would include employees among the company's shareholders.

Jaksic, who favoured international tenders, said he hoped the first round of privatisation would bring PTT between $1 and $2 billion. The money was seen being devoted to future development of telecommunications in Serbia.
"They will definitely move fast with this privatisation because the regime needs money urgently," the economist said.
President Slobodan Milosevic's Socialists have come under increasing pressure from foreign creditors and domestic opposition parties over the annulment of disputed election results last November 17.
The passage on Tuesday of a new law reinstating opposition gains in the municipal polls should ease the situation, but political analysts say the crisis is not yet over.
Serbia has not passed its privatisation law yet, but is expected to do so as soon as the parliament assembles for its first regular spring session.
There are plenty of reasons for PTT to be sold to foreign interests, another economist said.

"PTT's privatisation will upgrade and integrate Serbia with international telecommunications systems. PTT Srbija is a financially solid partner, regularly collecting payments on international phone calls," Jurij Bajec, an economics professor and member of the government expert team, told Reuters.
Bajec saw PTT Srbija's privatisation as a move encouraging other foreign investors to pour money into Serbia's ailing state sector.
But independent economists cautioned that in the absence of funds needed to finance its massive public spending, the government might use privatisation receipts.

"The current regime lacks around $110 million per month to pay wages, salaries and cover its costs. Some money is expected from privatisation of PTT Srbija and Zastava car producer. Only this year, sell-offs could bring Serbia between $700 million and $800 million at least," another economist said.
"Money is needed to keep the government intact and ready for the autumn elections," the economist said.
Analysts agreed it was difficult to estimate how foreigners would respond if the government used privatisation receipts to cover its public spending.
"But even foreigners will fish in murky waters to obtain a huge part of the cake -- Serbian telecom or car industry," an analyst said.
-- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
